papers.title: ECB caught in the French drama (Carsten Brzeski)
papers.summary: ECB expected on hold on 29 Oct. The jump in bond yields after the French crisis already tightens policy: German yields ~ a 25bp hike, France ~ 50bp. Next hike decision pushed to December (new projections). Path depends on Middle East war length, energy pass-through, and French contagion. Defences: dovish rates, flexible reinvestment (pause QT), then TPI, which is hard to justify while France is non-compliant with fiscal rules.

papers.title: FX Daily: Dollar has lost its safe-haven crown
papers.summary: Equities sold off on oil and AI worries; JPY and CHF were the safe-haven winners, not USD. Bond/equity negative correlation is back. UST 10y below 5%, 2y SOFR swap -15bp to 4.50%, but the bar to price out a December Fed hike is high. OAT-Bund 10y at 174bp (peak 178bp); EUR sensitivity to France can return quickly. CEE hit by risk-off (PLN, HUF vulnerable; EUR/HUF capped 368-370). MXN -8% since early Sept; Banxico dovish; USD/MXN 19.00-19.10 trajectory.

papers.title: Rates Spark: US and France like ships passing in the night at 5%
papers.summary: UST 10y broke below 5% on risk-off; ING expects it to revert above 5% (inflation, deficits, AI boom, US midterms), timing uncertain. French 10y above 5%, spread ~175bp vs Germany. Moody's (Aa3 negative) downgrade looks overdue, no fixed release time. A lasting French relief needs a credible 2027 budget, possibly not before December. Weak PMIs could trigger a bullish rates repricing and a more dovish ECB.

papers.title: The Commodities Feed: Brent builds geopolitical premium as Gulf risks rise
papers.summary: Brent +4% to just above $113/bbl on fears of renewed US-Iran escalation (reported strike consideration, second carrier, troop evacuations). ING's 4Q26 $80 average now looks unattainable; re-escalation seen as most likely path. TTF above EUR90/MWh (highest since Dec 2022); LNG largely absent this winter. Gold -2.8% toward $4,000 on inflation/policy worries; copper down on rising inventories and AI-stock selloff.

papers.title: October ECB cheat sheet: French malaise shouldn't prompt a dovish turn
papers.summary: ECB expected to hold at 2.5% on 29 Oct and keep the door open for a December hike, with a neutral, balanced message; a hike this week is priced near zero. Markets look for signs the French turmoil has triggered a dovish rethink - ING says not yet. EUR undervalued 1-1.5% vs short-term fair value; balance of risks still to the downside, but baseline is a broadly stable euro. ING preference: EUR/USD back to 1.120-1.130 in coming weeks. A surprise hike would risk a broader risk-off move, wider OAT spreads, lower equities and even lower Bund yields.

papers.title: FX Daily: Dollar buying returns ahead of FOMC
papers.summary: Dollar firmer at the start of the week as AI-related sentiment stabilises and markets position ahead of the FOMC; Chair Kevin Warsh reiterating inflation commitments reinforces the structural dollar floor. ING expects a broadly supported dollar this week. US consumer confidence seen at 81.5 (consensus 81.0) after 81.9 in September - soft data could dent hike pricing. Israeli election is tight; both Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs short of a majority, Eisenkot marginally more diplomatic on Iran. RBNZ expected to deliver a hawkish 25bp hike; NZD/USD 0.570 4Q forecast. CEE rates reconnecting with higher energy prices; CEE FX downside risk exceeds upside.

papers.title: Rates Spark: Temporary relief for structural problems
papers.summary: Moody's kept France at double-A (negative outlook), so the 10y OAT-Bund spread narrowed more than 10bp to below 155bp after being at its widest since 2011. Relief only - France still needs a significant, sustained fiscal effort, politics stay fragmented, elections are in April 2027, and a tail risk is support for Melenchon. For the ECB, the retightening removes some pressure to hike and lets officials keep constructive ambiguity. Elevated energy and resilient data outside France keep hawkish pressure on front-end rates.

papers.title: FX Daily: Can France wake up the ECB doves?
papers.summary: The softish dollar reaction to the Fed should not be over-read: the message stayed hawkish, a December hike is still 21bp priced and the bar to price it out is high. ING looked for core PCE at 0.3% MoM and 3Q GDP at 3.4% annualised, both dollar-positive, with DXY consolidating near the top of its range. On the ECB, the baseline was a neutral hold: not 'likely' to hike in December but 'possible/in play', with EUR/USD refusing to break 1.110. BoC hiked to 2.50% with more to come in 1Q27 and USD/CAD targeted at 1.420; the CNB looks set to go to 4.00% next week, and TTF above EUR100 keeps ING bearish on CEE currencies.

papers.title: Fed holds rates steady despite inflation being too high
papers.summary: The FOMC held at 3.75-4.00% on a 10-2 vote, with Hammack and Cook dissenting for a hike (Cook's vote was the surprise given her centrist record). The statement kept 'inflation remains elevated' and 'expanding at a strong pace' with no pre-commitment; Warsh offered no guidance beyond promising price stability 'no ifs, ands or buts'. A December hike to 4.00-4.25% stays ING's call, with two payroll reports and a CPI print before the decision. ING expects US inflation back at 2% in 2H27, a prolonged pause through 2027 and the December 2026 hike reversed in December 2027; from September one FOMC meeting a year will carry no rate vote, two from 2028.

papers.title: Rates Spark: Leaning hawkish, but no action
papers.summary: The hawkish lean was enough to validate the 10y back above 5%; there was barely a word in the statement that did not lean hawkish, yet no hike. Warsh's comforting line on inflation expectations pulled yields back to 5%, but expectations actually rose after the decision, and ING maintains the journey toward 5.25% while the front end likes the hold, steepening the curve from both ends. Balance-sheet run-off stays a Warsh objective but is not imminent; repo liquidity is stable. For the ECB, 23bp of December tightening is already priced, so the France questions at the press conference mattered more than the decision, with a high hurdle for a QT pause or TPI.

papers.title: FX Daily: Abatement in AI risk helps the dollar
papers.summary: SK Hynix delivered strong earnings and Nasdaq futures added 0.6%, easing the AI-credit fear that had been the main threat to the bullish dollar story, so FX attention went back to energy, inflation and central banks. DXY is edging to the year's highs, where 102.50 opens 103.00. EUR/USD sits at the year's lows with 1.1065/1.1110 key support and 1.0880 the technical target below it, and the ECB bank lending survey showed tighter conditions plus an unexpected fall in corporate loan demand. A 20bp gilt risk premium could partly unwind on a boring UK budget, keeping EUR/GBP heavy toward 0.8315, and the BoC call was a coin flip.

papers.title: The Commodities Feed: European gas tops EUR100 as supply fears grow
papers.summary: TTF settled 4.85% higher and broke above EUR100/MWh for the first time since 2022, with little sign of relief in Persian Gulf LNG flows. QatarEnergy has extended force majeure for several buyers to the end of the year, Norwegian unplanned outages add supply risk and northwest Europe faces colder-than-usual weather from next week, with EU storage just under 75% and winter draws still ahead. Demand destruction is starting: power is deep into gas-to-coal switching and Yara has curtailed European ammonia, cutting its European gas use more than 7% YoY in 3Q26. Funds added 14.3TWh to their TTF net long, taking it to 207.4TWh.

papers.title: The Commodities Feed: Oil in wait-and-see mode ahead of US midterms
papers.summary: Crude fell for a second day with Brent still around $114, as the market waits for clarity on Trump's next move on Iran and will likely stay in wait-and-see until after the 3 November midterms. A US-Iran deal is not needed for prices to fall: simply getting past the elections without renewed strikes could start eroding the risk premium. Products are loosening - Russia lifted its diesel export ban and the ICE gasoil crack slid toward $70, its lowest since early October - and there are tentative signs of Russia-Ukraine diplomacy. API showed US crude stocks down about 2m barrels; gold recovered above $4,000, copper tightened on a record Yangshan premium and LME backwardation, while iron ore hit a two-year low.

papers.title: RBNZ's huge dovish surprise spells trouble for Kiwi dollar
papers.summary: The RBNZ held at 2.75% on a 4-3 vote when markets priced 23bp of hikes, and NZD fell 1.4%; the dovish bloc, including Governor Breman, argued 3Q inflation was lower than expected and that growth risks dominate. With inflation set to break above 4% in 4Q26, a December hold would leave the real policy rate at -1.4%. ING still expects a hike in December (22bp priced) and at least one more in 1Q27, and sees pricing beyond that as too aggressive (60bp by March, 100bp by August 2027). NZD outperformance is dropped: year-end NZD/USD stays 0.570 but with downside risk, and AUD/NZD above 1.260 looks imminent after a hot Australian CPI.

papers.title: Bank of Canada likely to hike again after today's move
papers.summary: The BoC raised its overnight rate 25bp to 2.50% with about 80% priced and economists split; it justified the move with stronger-than-expected growth, solid consumer spending, rebounding oil-and-gas capex and sectors hit by US tariffs strengthening, while unemployment has risen to 6.5%. Cost pass-through could become a 2027 theme, so there 'could be the need to increase the policy rate further', but the BoC will 'proceed carefully'. ING targets 2.75% in 1Q27 (January preferred) with a December hike as the risk, and judges the 90bp of tightening priced over 12 months as too hawkish. CAD stays oil-dependent with a 1.420 year-end USD/CAD target.

papers.title: Rates Spark: Kevin Warsh and John Healey walk into a bar
papers.summary: About 20bp of risk premium sits in the 10y gilt ahead of the Autumn Budget, versus near zero a few months ago, and a boring budget could unwind most of it after gilts held up well in the pre-budget auctions. Global factors still drive sterling rates, and an early election would be the next surprise. In the US, the 10y had been clinging to 4.99% waiting to tick the FOMC off before deviating from 5%, and ING expects it to snap back above 5% on inflation, the deficit and the AI boom; a super-hawkish Warsh without a hike would tempt that, a super-dovish one would validate the break below. Balance-sheet shrinkage plans are expected nearer the turn of the year.

papers.title: ECB keeps rates on hold as Christine Lagarde announced her resignation
papers.summary: The ECB left rates unchanged because higher headline inflation is showing few knock-on effects while bond yields have already made financing conditions more restrictive - the bond market has taken over the ECB's job. The news came hours earlier: Lagarde announced she will step down on 7 February 2027. France dominates the TPI debate, because the instrument requires compliance with the EU fiscal framework and that is hard to argue for France today; ING hopes the ECB remembers March 2020, when saying it was not there to narrow spreads backfired. (Snap: filed outside the three tracked sections.)

papers.title: Lagarde's comments point to a December ECB rate hike
papers.summary: Rates on hold and Lagarde out is the headline, but the nuance is that the ECB still looks set to hike in December despite growing stagflationary pressures: it debated a hike today and the worsening of financing conditions took it off the table. Lagarde called growth risks tilted to the downside and inflation risks to the upside, saw no second-round effects beyond the September projections, and flagged two developments since September - higher energy prices and tighter financing conditions. ING's three parameters are the length of the Middle East war, the pass-through of energy into the rest of the economy, and French contagion.

papers.title: Eurozone sentiment weakens in October as price expectations tick up
papers.summary: The eurozone Economic Sentiment Indicator fell to 96.9 from 97.5, the weakest since June, with employment expectations up slightly. Industry actually improved - production, orders and hiring intentions all firmer - while services were more downbeat on demand but more optimistic on the months ahead; consumers are shying away from major purchases. The ECB-relevant detail is that both industry and services expect stronger price increases ahead, especially for goods. No immediate need to hike, but no room to sound dovish either. (Snap: filed outside the three tracked sections.)

papers.title: ING webinar on the 2027 rates outlook: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly
papers.summary: ING's 2027 rates webinar (4 November, 1400 GMT) frames the debate rather than taking a view: whether the US 10y can reach 6% on AI and productivity, extraordinary deficits and stubborn inflation, what Treasury Secretary Bessent could do if yields surge, and whether the eurozone's inflation shock is changing rather than fading. It also asks how second-round effects, heavy bond supply and rising global real rates complicate the ECB's path even if it turns more dovish, with France's debt challenge as the extra sovereign uncertainty. Useful as the agenda for what to watch into year-end.

papers.title: A strong economy may not be enough to sway Spain's election
papers.summary: Spain's 29 November election has been overshadowed by a fatal high-speed rail collision near Urda in Toledo province that killed at least 69 people and led most parties to suspend campaigning, putting rail safety and public services into the debate alongside corruption cases touching the Socialists. The economy is still outperforming - 3Q GDP rose 0.6% QoQ and 2.7% YoY, well above most large eurozone peers - but unemployment climbed from 9.87% to 10.18% as the labour force grew 169,500 against 73,600 new jobs, harmonised inflation held at 4.9% and retail sales fell 1.4% YoY in September. The People's Party leads the polls and could reach a majority with Vox; Feijoo promises one million homes and a new Land Law within 100 days, against Socialist rent limits and eviction protection, while Spain added ~1.22m households between 2021 and 2025 but completed only ~466,000 homes. ING sees limited near-term macro impact - the energy shock and monetary tightening matter more - but a fragmented parliament would prolong the budget extensions and legislative paralysis.

papers.title: FX Daily: Time to think about the midterms?
papers.summary: Fresh pressure on tech stocks drove safe-haven demand into Treasuries and weighed on the dollar, and ING sees precautionary unwinding of net-long dollar positions as the main risk into Tuesday's midterms, with a Democratic sweep around 68% in prediction markets read as mildly dollar-negative through shutdown and debt-ceiling gridlock. Thursday's US data leaned hawkish - 3Q growth 3.4% and September core PCE 0.3% MoM - and the FOMC blackout ends with Barkin (neutral), Daly (moderate dove) and Musalem (moderate hawk), though ING doubts they can add much with a December hike priced. Lagarde said a hike was discussed, gave no indication French bonds prompt a dovish rethink and officials are 'ready' to raise in December, leaving room for EUR/USD to re-test 1.120-1.1250; ING expects eurozone 3Q GDP at 0.3% QoQ but only 0% in France against 0.1% consensus, and a negative French print would widen spreads. The BoJ held at 1.25% and flagged its 2% target as met, with ING now looking for hikes in December and March/April and USD/JPY holding a 155-160 range.

papers.title: Bank of Japan hits 2% price target
papers.summary: The BoJ left the policy rate at 1.25% - back-to-back hikes would have upset markets - but said for the first time that underlying CPI is 'generally consistent' with the 2% target set in 2013, so the debate shifts to how fast it reaches a 1.75-2.00% neutral rate. Energy prices, AI demand and the weak yen were all named as upside inflation risks, growth forecasts were held around 0.7-0.8%, CPI forecasts were nudged higher and the BoJ acknowledged overseas rate rises, with an implicit fear that not matching December hikes from the Fed and ECB would leave the yen vulnerable. ING now expects 25bp hikes in December and March, a 1.75% policy rate ahead of April consumption support, and an acceleration of ETF sales from JPY330bn to JPY860bn a year from 2027. USD/JPY stays bid toward the top of 155-160 until a decisive turn lower in 2Q27, with a USD/KRW-style AI-driven upside surprise the one to watch in 2027.

papers.title: Rates Spark: Hikes coming, but bond yields choosing to fall
papers.summary: The US 10y made a decisive gap away from 5%, but to the downside, even though September core PCE rose to 3.1% - far from the 2% Warsh keeps restating - and income, spending and jobless claims all came in firm; the 7yr auction cleared with no tail and decent demand, and the move was more a back-end than front-end story. ING reads it as Treasuries staying responsive to AI-valuation sentiment and equity wobbles rather than fundamentals, calls it contrary to its preferred path back to higher yields but not enough to change its tune. On the ECB, a December hike looks near-certain with more than 20bp priced unless the Middle East improves or French bonds deteriorate, and a Reuters report that ECB staff see higher yields cutting 2027-28 growth by 100bp and inflation by 90bp supports ING's view that December could be the last hike of the cycle. Market pricing for further ECB tightening over 12 months has already fallen toward 65bp, driven mainly by French risk-off and more recently AI jitters, while Friday brings French, Spanish and German CPI plus eurozone 3Q GDP.

papers.title: FX Daily: Dollar holds gains into midterms
papers.summary: The dollar was fractionally lower to start the week, tracking oil 2-3% lower on reports that Trump wants to let diplomacy run its course with Iran, while betting sites give the Democrats a 70-72% chance of taking both chambers in Tuesday's midterms - an outcome ING calls mildly dollar-negative on debt-ceiling gridlock and a prolonged shutdown next year, but largely speculative against 3Q growth of 3.4%, a sixth consecutive year of above-target inflation and a Fed readying another hike. DXY should keep trading around 102.00 with no strong case for a correction lower, with ISM surveys and Friday's October payrolls mattering less than price data barring a disastrous report. The 9% Nasdaq sell-off last month has softened short-dated US rates and a further tech slide is the biggest risk to long dollar positioning, with Apple reporting after today's close. Fitch's unscheduled late-Friday move of France's A+ outlook to negative, with another review promised by end-February, should cap EUR/USD rebounds - sellers are suspected in the 1.1200/1.1250 area - and keep EUR/CHF pressed toward 0.9180/85; a 25bp BoE hike to 4.00% on Thursday looks fully priced, the CNB is set to hike 25bp to 4.00%, and the NBP is expected to hold at 3.75% with no hike before 1Q27.

papers.title: The Commodities Feed: US midterm elections key for oil market
papers.summary: ICE Brent settled almost 2.4% higher on Friday to close above $113/bbl, with the expiring Dec-26 contract at $117.64 on its last trading day, but prices are off 2-3% today on reports that Trump wants to give diplomacy a chance and as Iranian negotiators hold talks with Qatari mediators in Doha. If the midterms pass with neither US/Israeli strikes nor a deal, the question is whether the geopolitical premium keeps being priced or starts to unwind, and with the speculative ICE Brent net long up 3,576 lots to 245,457 lots - still well below March's ~430k peak - there is room to add on the right catalyst. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries resumed after a roughly two-week pause that had taken the ICE gasoil crack below $70/bbl, Russia plans to export 2.15m tonnes of diesel in November against just over 500kt in October, and OPEC+ kept December output targets unchanged with most members already producing below target. TTF settled more than 6% higher near EUR104/MWh with colder-than-usual NW European weather ahead and storage just under 75% after peaking last Tuesday; gold fell 3.65% to a one-year low of $3,874.62/oz with silver down more than 6%, copper slipped although the LME cash-3m backwardation at $174.85/t and a Yangshan premium above $200/t show physical tightness, and CBOT corn lost nearly 11% in October on harvest pressure with the speculative net long cut for a sixth week to 55,314 lots.

papers.title: Bank of England set for first rate hike as energy shock worsens
papers.summary: The BoE is set to hike 25bp to 4.00% on 5 November - its first move since the Iran war began, after an 'active hold' that stood in for 50bp of cuts - because a circa 25% January rise in the household energy cap pushes CPI to peak just above 4% early next year, with ING seeing a follow-up in February as more likely than not. It would be an insurance hike: there is no sign of second-round effects, energy-intensive inflation has actually fallen this year, core services are well behaved, private-sector wage growth is 3.4% and the labour market is stabilising. Watch the vote split (Dhingra and Taylor are the known doves, with Breeden the likeliest extra dissenter), guidance the Bank is expected to keep as non-committal as possible, and whether anyone pushes back on more than four hikes priced by this time next year - Huw Pill has already suggested that pricing looks unlikely. Global factors now explain less of GBP rate moves and UK swaps stay positively correlated with oil, so a big repricing is unlikely and sterling's outperformance can continue with EUR/GBP consolidating after a near-4% drop in just over a month.

papers.title: German inflation drops to 2.8% YoY in October
papers.summary: German headline inflation fell to 2.8% YoY in October from 3.3% and core inflation to 2.1% from 2.4%, a broader retreat than the fuel tax rebate alone, with services inflation also lower, household energy prices down month-on-month and no sign of indirect effects from higher energy prices at state level. ING still expects headline inflation back above 3% into late 2026 and early 2027 on oil, the winter heating season and low gas storage, and says it could take until end-2027 before it drops below 2% again - but selling price expectations remain below their April-May levels and consumers have less willingness and ability to pay than in 2022, so margin squeezing rather than pass-through is the expectation. For the ECB the numbers comfort the doves: with no second-round effects in sight, even a December hike might not yet be a done deal. (Snap: filed outside the three tracked sections.)

papers.title: Riksbank to hike despite soft inflation and rallying krona
papers.summary: The Riksbank is expected to hike 25bp to 2.00% on 4 November even though market bets have slipped from 22-24bp to 15-18bp, with officials' in-meeting and off-meeting commentary endorsing a move and the energy shock outweighing September's soft print and the stronger krona; no explicit commitment to more should follow, but the tightening bias stays. CPIF came in at 1.5% YoY as expected while CPIF excluding energy was just 0.5%, 0.2ppt below the Riksbank's forecast, though goods inflation was broad-based with durable prices up 1.1% month-on-month; ING keeps CPIF at 2.5% in December and expects a further hike to 2.25% on 3 February, after which the risks are hawkish. Brent is $118 against the $92 end-2026 assumption from September and European gas is up around 35%, while the krona is only 1.4% stronger on a trade-weighted basis and still 4% weaker year-to-date, so a hold would invite fresh SEK weakness. ING cuts its year-end EUR/SEK target to 11.00 from 11.10-11.15, sees a possible break below 10.90 in the coming week and a gradual slide to 10.70 over the next year.

papers.title: Rates Spark: Bank of England likely to join the hiking club
papers.summary: Euro rates liked the oil move, with Brent sliding well below $100/bbl, front-end inflation swaps dropping and the money market now pricing only a little more than 50bp of ECB tightening by summer next year - though October headline inflation still rose to 4%. Bunds rallied with 10y yields below 3.3% and the 10y OAT/Bund spread easing below 150bp, tighter by more than 10bp on the day, which ING had expected towards year-end on a 2027 budget showing some deficit consolidation (even by decree) but not beyond it, given the presidential election. ING is less convinced than the market about the need for almost three more BoE hikes after today's 24bp-priced move, and sees a big repricing lower for GBP rates once inflation dynamics improve by mid-2027. Today brings French September industrial production (consensus -0.3% YoY), eurozone September PPI at +10.6% YoY and Spanish and French auctions of €6.75bn and €12bn.

papers.title: FX Daily: A dollar downturn lacks the rate ingredient
papers.summary: The Democratic sweep delivered the dollar-negative move ING expected but no case for more, because lower oil is not unequivocally dollar-negative: with crude down 8%, 2y USD swap rates fell only 5bp while EUR, GBP and NZD 2y swaps fell 8-10bp, leaving DXY favoured to stabilise at 101.0-101.50. US data still support Fed tightening - ISM services employment rose to 51.4, the highest since February, and ADP payrolls at 86k point to a robust print against a 65k consensus - while a Banxico cut could push USD/MXN to 19. Knot came out firmly hawkish after the Netherlands backed his ECB candidacy, arguing second-round effects will pick up, while eurozone October inflation rose to 4.0% as expected with core anchored at 2.5%, making at least one December ECB hike look a done deal and leaving little upside in EUR/USD beyond the 1.130 year-end target. The BoE is expected to hike 25bp to 4.00% today on a 7-2 vote with a February follow-up as the base case, EUR/GBP stabilising near 0.840 and cable capped at 1.350, while Norges Bank holds at 4.5% and Sweden's October CPIF slows to 1.1% with the ex-energy measure at 0.1% after yesterday's hike.

papers.title: France’s manufacturing rebound offers some relief, but no turning point yet
papers.summary: French manufacturing output rose 0.5% in September after 0.3% in August, back to its June level, with food up 1.0%, electrical and computer equipment up 2.6% to the highest since November 2023 and transport equipment up 2.7% on a 7.5% rebound in autos - but output is still 0.9% below a year earlier, autos are down 9.3% YoY and total industrial production fell 0.5% on lower electricity output. Construction remains in deep recession, down another 0.2% in September and 4.5% below a year ago (civil engineering -6.6%, building -4.8%), and credit is tightening harder than anywhere else in the eurozone, with a net 27% of French banks stricter on business loans in 3Q. ING keeps GDP at 0.3% for 2026 and 0.5% for 2027 with risks to the downside, and notes the National Assembly unanimously rejected the revenue side of the 2027 budget by 458 votes after 11 days of debate, with adopted amendments pushing the deficit to an estimated 5.9% of GDP against the 5% target and only the Senate, Article 49.3 or a budget by ordinance before the 70-day deadline left.

papers.title: US rates and a triple whammy of obstacles to overcome
papers.summary: ING's 2027 US rates baseline is a 10y Treasury yield back to 5.25%-plus (from 4.9% now) in the first quarter, with the absolute upside capped at 5.5%, as AI-sparked productivity growth, elevated fiscal deficits and sticky inflation keep the real yield and the term premium rising. Beyond the first quarter it looks for inflation to ease enough for the Fed to step away and the market to re-discount cuts, taking the 10y to 4.75% and then 4.5-4.75%, and flags three uncalled routes to 6%: GDP growth of 3-4%, a deficit blowing out to 7-8% of GDP, or inflation stuck around 3%. It prefers to fade the swap-spread tightening - the 10y swap spread below 40bp should re-widen above 50bp through 2027 and the 30y to at least 75bp - unless Treasury Secretary Bessent materially cuts long-end issuance or adds to buybacks.

papers.title: The grand Dutch pension reform finale
papers.summary: Dutch pension reform reaches its finale with almost €900bn of assets scheduled to transition in January 2027 on top of roughly €600bn already moved in 2026, out of a system holding more than €1.5tr. Because hedges will be set by age cohort rather than at fund level - just 10% for younger participants against 75% for those close to retirement - demand for hedges beyond 25 years will be relatively small, so the 10s30s euro swap curve should steepen structurally; ING credits the reforms with some 20bp of the 2025 steepening, while this year's flattening was a hawkish ECB and Fed repricing. The January transition should be orderly given funding ratios well above the 105% threshold (ABP above 130%), but hedging needs now move with asset prices, so funds will have to rebalance more often than under the old once-a-year liability review.

papers.title: The Good the Bad and the Ugly for Rates in 2027
papers.summary: ING's 2027 outlook centres on the good, the bad and the ugly causing trouble through at least the first quarter, taking the 10y Treasury back above 5.25% (capped at 5.5%) before inflation eases enough for a move to 4.5-4.75% later in the year. Euro rates get a bumpy ride in which a benign outcome brings the 2y swap down some 50bp while the 10y stays sticky, and an ugly inflation outcome could push the 10y well above 4%. European spreads face a turbulent first half with France the fault line and Bunds' safe-haven appeal masking supply, sterling rates sit well above fair value but only reprice significantly lower once the BoE can prove inflation is heading back to target by end-2027, and the Dutch pension finale should keep the 10s30s euro swap curve structurally steeper.

papers.title: Rates Spark: A blue wave in the US and euro inflation
papers.summary: A decisive Democratic victory removes the risk of a contested result and of a Congress split between the parties, which should support sentiment, but the Democrats campaigned on a firmer anti-free-market line on data centres - and with much of US growth relying on the AI boom, stricter policy could become a headwind to watch. With Trump still running foreign policy inflation remains a wild card: the Iran war is not over, oil barely budged on the result and tariffs could return, and implied volatility measures suggest preparing for significant rate moves. Eurozone flash October CPI is seen at 4.0% headline with core steady at 2.5%, still pointing to a December ECB hike, with the ECB wage tracker and Lane speaking, while the US gets ISM services (seen 54.8), ADP and the quarterly refunding announcement with no change to coupon issuance expected.

papers.title: FX Daily: Blue wave price action a preview of what's to come
papers.summary: The blue wave first hit AI-sensitive assets - Korean and Taiwanese equities fell 3-4% overnight - but those losses were fully recouped once investors noted the Democrats do not take office until January and Trump accepted the results, leaving US 2y yields holding most of their 8-9bp drop and the overnight DXY low of 101.25 as important support into Friday's payrolls. ING still reads a Democratic Congress as mildly dollar-negative via the AI story and a possible prolonged shutdown from next summer, but with a strong US economy and a Fed ready to tighten it will not chase the dollar lower now; EUR/USD is correcting from a 1.1260 spike that marks the top of the range ahead of flash CPI (headline 4.0%, core 2.5%), where an upside core surprise would be euro-positive. Swiss October inflation at a surprisingly high 1.5% raises questions over whether the SNB can avoid tightening through 2027, a clean franc positive with downside risk to EUR/CHF, while the Riksbank's hike to 2.0% keeps its tightening bias and EUR/SEK around 11.00.

papers.title: France’s social demands run up against tightening fiscal constraints
papers.summary: Between 320,000 and 500,000 people marched last Saturday and all the main unions mobilise on 5 November over wages and purchasing power, pushing a government that is already considering a discretionary minimum-wage rise of 0.5-0.6pp on top of January's automatic ~1% - the first since 2012 - even though private-sector employment has fallen for seven straight quarters, 0.3% lower YoY and almost 70,000 jobs lost. After ten days and more than 2,300 amendments the 2027 budget is drifting towards a wider deficit than planned: the revenue vote was postponed again, adopted amendments have already worsened the projected deficit by €23.9bn (the 2026 total will be around €165bn), and with the National Assembly unlikely to approve anything the government faces Article 49.3 or, once the 70-day deadline expires on 18 December, a budget by ordinance. The 5% target is unrealistic on 1% growth assumptions given 3Q GDP fell 0.1%, investment dropped 0.6%, consumer confidence slid five points to 80 (lowest since June 2013) and a net 27% of banks tightened credit, so ING sees 0.3% growth this year and 0.5% in 2027, a deficit near 5.5% of GDP, debt above the 121.7% forecast for 2027 and a 10y OAT at 4.9%, more than 155bp over Bund against 70bp at end-2025.

papers.title: European bond spreads in a duel with the 'Bad'
papers.summary: Eurozone sovereign spreads are back in focus not just as country stories but as a function of rate volatility and risk sentiment, and the bad - high deficits - has re-entered the narrative with France singled out while Spain votes this month, Italy goes before the end of next year, Finland votes and Germany faces five state elections. ING sees the 10y OAT/Bund spread holding around 150bp as a floor through the electoral uncertainty around the 18 April and 2 May 2027 presidential rounds, with a tail risk that support for Mélenchon (who has floated cancelling the debt held by the Banque de France) pushes it beyond 200bp, and warns spreads could stay well above 100bp even afterwards alongside further downgrades - the market already prices France as if rated BBB. The ECB is likely to let markets work while the stress stays French, dialling back hawkishness or suspending QT rather than deploying TPI whose bar is high by the 500bp-plus BTP precedent of 2011, and Germany's safe-haven bid should fade as gross Bund funding exceeds €400bn next year plus at least €80bn of ECB runoff, taking 10y Bunds to at least 20bp over OIS from around 13bp.

papers.title: Euro rates have good reason to be nervous
papers.summary: ING's 2027 euro rates view pairs substantial near-term upside risk with a more constructive year-end: ugly second-round inflation fears could take the 10y euro swap above 4% while faster disinflation could take it to 2%, and the baseline has inflation pressures easing and the ECB terminal rate anchoring near 2.5% by end-2027, with the 2y swap some 50bp lower if all goes well. Oil no longer tells the story - even at below $80/bbl swap rates would find little immediate relief - so each inflation print is watched for second-round effects, and with the 1Y1Y forward at just 2.2% and three further ECB hikes priced, a perceived weakening of transmission plus upside surprises could add another 100bp to 2y swaps. The 10y swap should stay sticky near fair value against nominal growth expectations of 3.3% as global real rates and heavy supply rise, with France the risk that forces the ECB to keep conditions supportive, halt QT and tolerate higher inflation - steeper curves, and the ECB caving to inflation is an unpriced risk with 5y5y swaps at just 2.1%.

papers.title: A delayed landing for GBP rates
papers.summary: ING expects the 10y gilt to ease in 2027 as inflation fears abate and the BoE starts considering cuts, but the path lower will be volatile because the 10y GBP swap is almost perfectly explained (98%) by BoE expectations plus the level and 2s10s slope of the US curve. Forwards already imply at least 100bp of further hikes to a ~4.75% terminal rate, above what is priced for the Fed, and ING disagrees - it sees a risk premium in the front end beyond macro fundamentals, so 2y GBP rates ease into 1H27 with the bigger dovish turn in the second half once inflation gives confidence of a return to 2%. QT tweaks that keep gilts of 23 years or longer on the balance sheet relieve the 30y, but the rise in long yields is a global trend and the extra supply is being absorbed by price-sensitive buyers - banks only partially, insurers and pension funds playing a smaller role - which keeps a material term premium justified.

stories.name: French fiscal crisis and the ECB
stories.summary: The 2027 budget is going nowhere except towards a wider deficit: after eleven days the National Assembly rejected the revenue side unanimously by 458 votes, adopted amendments have already added €23.9bn (taking the deficit to an estimated 5.9% of GDP against the 5% target), and with the 70-day deadline expiring on 18 December the government's only routes are Article 49.3 or a budget by ordinance. Unions mobilise on 5 November over wages and purchasing power while growth stays near zero - 3Q GDP fell 0.1%, consumer confidence dropped five points to 80 and a net 27% of banks tightened credit - and ING sees just 0.3% growth this year and 0.5% in 2027, a deficit near 5.5% of GDP and debt above the 121.7% forecast, with the 10y OAT at 4.9% and more than 155bp over Bund against 70bp at end-2025. Fitch's unscheduled move of the A+ outlook to negative is now compounded by a spread market pricing France as if rated BBB; ING sees 150bp OAT/Bund as a floor through the 18 April and 2 May 2027 presidential rounds with a Mélenchon tail beyond 200bp, and expects the ECB to let markets work - the TPI bar is high. Eurozone October inflation at 4.0% with core at 2.5% keeps a December ECB hike on track and the succession (Knot hawkish, de Cos the dove) is the other EUR lever.

The lower price is already doing macro work: front-end euro inflation swaps have dropped, the market prices only a little more than 50bp of ECB tightening by summer 2027 and ING's 2027 outlooks assume oil below $80/bbl. The physical buffer is thinner than the price action implies, with the ICE Brent net long far below March's peak and renewed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries holding the gasoil crack up, and Norway's krone is the clearest casualty as ING sees EUR/NOK back to 10.50 and ending the year at 10.55-10.65.

stories.name: US rates, Fed hike risk and AI-valuation wobble
stories.summary: The blue wave delivered exactly the mild dollar-negative move ING expected - US 2y yields fell 8-9bp and DXY touched 101.25 before stabilising, with ING seeing a 101.0-101.50 base rather than another break lower because lower oil is not unequivocally dollar-negative and US data still argue for tightening (ADP 86k, ISM services employment at 51.4, payrolls consensus 65k). The 2027 call is for the 10y Treasury back above 5.25% and possibly 5.5% in the first quarter on AI-sparked productivity, deficits and sticky inflation, then 4.5-4.75% later in the year as inflation eases and cuts are re-discounted - with three plausible routes to 6% - and for 10y swap spreads to re-widen above 50bp. Sterling rates sit above ING's fair value with the market pricing at least 100bp of further BoE hikes to a 4.75% terminal rate that ING rejects, and the BoE is expected to hike 25bp to 4.00% today on a 7-2 vote with a February follow-up as the base case. The AI angle cuts both ways: Korean and Taiwanese equities fell 3-4% on the result before recouping, and the Democrats' firmer line on data centres is a policy headwind for the capex boom.

changelog.text: Batch 1: four ING articles (22-23 Oct 2026) analysed; four stories created. Probabilities are initial estimates.

France: Moody's kept France at double-A (negative outlook) instead of downgrading; OAT-Bund tightened >10bp to <155bp from an 11-year wide. Contained-stress probability raised 55% -> 62%, contagion cut 25% -> 20%, relief cut 15% -> 13%.

ECB: the 29 Oct meeting is now framed as a hold at 2.5% with the door open for December, not a debate about hiking now. Baseline is a neutral message and a broadly stable euro, with EUR/USD targeted at 1.120-1.130.

USD: the narrative flipped this week. Last week the dollar had 'lost its safe-haven crown'; now stabilising AI sentiment and pre-FOMC positioning have brought dollar buying back. Hawkish-Fed scenario raised 25% -> 30%, AI risk-off cut 25% -> 22%.

Oil: no new commodity note, but the Israeli election is a fresh de-escalation channel (Eisenkot softer on Iran than Netanyahu). De-escalation 15% -> 18%, re-escalation 38% -> 36%, supply outage 7% -> 6%.

Removed the 'EM and CEE FX under pressure' story at your request. The source detail (MXN, PLN, HUF, RON) is still recorded inside the papers, and ING still flags CEE FX downside risk in this week's FX Daily.
Still open: FOMC tomorrow, ECB on 29 Oct, RBNZ (hawkish 25bp expected), US consumer confidence today.

Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on a 10-2 vote: Hammack and Cook dissented for a hike, and Warsh promised price stability 'no ifs, ands or buts' without pre-committing to December. A hike to 4.00-4.25% stays ING's call with 21bp priced. Hawkish-Fed scenario raised 30% -> 34%, choppy base cut 43% -> 41%.
The AI risk-off impulse faded: SK Hynix beat, Nasdaq futures added 0.6% and Alphabet/Microsoft reported next. AI-led risk-off and growth scare cut 22% -> 20%.

ECB held on 29 Oct as expected. Lagarde framed it as the bond market taking over the ECB's job, saw growth risks to the downside and inflation risks to the upside, and still pointed to a December hike.

Christine Lagarde announced she will step down on 7 February 2027 - a snap filed outside the three tracked sections, picked up by the macro layer. Contagion/ECB-backstop raised 20% -> 22%, disorderly raised 5% -> 6%, contained stress cut 62% -> 60%, French relief cut 13% -> 12%.

Oil: Brent around $114 and lower for a second day into the 3 November midterms; Russia lifted its diesel export ban and the ICE gasoil crack fell to ~$70. De-escalation raised 18% -> 22%, re-escalation cut 36% -> 32%.

Gas: TTF settled above EUR100/MWh for the first time since 2022 (+4.85%) on extended Qatari force majeure, Norwegian outages and colder weather; EU storage just under 75%. Elevated-premium scenario held at 40%.
Eurozone sentiment fell to 96.9 from 97.5, but industry and services both expect stronger price increases ahead, so no hike is needed now and no dovish turn is available either.
RBNZ held at 2.75% on a 4-3 vote and NZD fell 1.4%; BoC hiked 25bp to 2.50% with ING seeing a 2.75% peak in 1Q27. USD/CAD keeps a 1.420 year-end target and markets look too hawkish on both.
Still open: BoJ on 30 Oct, US midterms 3 November, ING 2027 rates webinar 4 November, and payrolls plus CPI before the 9 December FOMC. UK Autumn Budget gilt reaction also pending.

Rates Spark: the US 10y gapped decisively away from 5% to the downside even though September core PCE rose to 3.1% and income, spending and claims were firm; the 7yr auction cleared with no tail and the move was concentrated at the back end. ING keeps its 5.25% call. Hawkish-Fed scenario cut 34% -> 32%.

AI sentiment is the marginal driver of Treasuries and the dollar again: fresh pressure on tech stocks brought haven flows, and a Democratic sweep is ~68% priced for the 3 November midterms, which ING reads as mildly dollar-negative and a reason not to chase USD upside. AI-led risk-off and growth scare raised 20% -> 24%, choppy base cut 41% -> 39% as the 10y left 5% behind.

ECB: Lagarde confirmed a hike was discussed, gave no sign French bonds prompt a dovish rethink and officials are 'ready' to raise in December with 20bp+ priced; a Reuters report has ECB staff estimating higher yields cut 2027-28 growth by 100bp and inflation by 90bp, keeping December as the likely last hike of the cycle. Contained-grinding-stress raised 60% -> 61%, French relief cut 12% -> 11%.

BoJ held at 1.25% but for the first time judged underlying CPI consistent with the 2% target, naming energy, AI demand and the weak yen as upside risks. ING now expects 25bp hikes in December and March, a 1.75% policy rate by April and ETF sales accelerated to JPY860bn a year from 2027, with USD/JPY bid in 155-160 until a 2Q27 turn lower.

Spain's 29 November election is a close race with the PP ahead and a PP-Vox majority possible; 3Q GDP grew 0.6% QoQ and 2.7% YoY but unemployment rose to 10.18% and harmonised inflation held at 4.9%, and ING sees little immediate macro impact. Filed under the france-ecb story as eurozone political risk; no probability change.

No commodities paper in this batch, so oil-iran weights are unchanged: Brent near $114 and TTF above EUR100 still hold the premium, with renewed speculation about US strikes on Iran offset by looser product markets and the lifted Russian diesel ban.

Still open: US midterms 3 November, Spain's election 29 November, eurozone flash CPI and 3Q GDP (France 0% expected against 0.1% consensus, a negative print would widen spreads), ING's 2027 rates webinar 4 November, Lagarde's successor announcement (de Cos dove vs Knot hawk), BoJ hikes in December and March, and payrolls plus CPI before the 9 December FOMC.

FX Daily: Democrats are 70-72% priced to take both chambers on 3 November, which ING calls mildly dollar-negative but speculative against 3Q growth of 3.4%, a sixth year of above-target inflation and a Fed readying another hike, with DXY holding around 102.00 and no case for a correction lower. The bigger risk to long-dollar positioning is the tech sell-off - Nasdaq fell 9% last month, Apple reports tonight and gold slid 3.65% to a one-year low of $3,874.62/oz as investors raise cash. AI-led risk-off and growth scare raised 24% -> 25%, choppy base cut 39% -> 38%.

Fitch moved its outlook on France's A+ sovereign rating from stable to negative in an unscheduled review late Friday and promised another review by end-February, citing the failure to repair public finances in weak growth; ING sees it capping EUR/USD rebounds (sellers suspected at 1.1200/1.1250) and keeping EUR/CHF pressed toward 0.9180/85. Contained-grinding-stress raised 61% -> 62%, French relief cut 11% -> 10%.

German inflation snap (macro layer): headline fell to 2.8% YoY in October from 3.3% and core to 2.1% from 2.4%, with services lower, household energy down MoM on the fuel tax rebate and no indirect energy effects at state level; ING still sees headline back above 3% into early 2027 and says even a December ECB hike may not be a done deal. The dovish comfort is offset by the Fitch move, so contagion/ECB-backstop stays at 22% and disorderly at 6%.

Commodities Feed: Brent settled 2.4% higher on Friday just above $113 (Dec-26 expiry $117.64) but is down 2-3% today on reports Trump wants to let diplomacy with Iran run, with Iranian negotiators in Doha; Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries resumed after a two-week pause, Russia plans 2.15m t of November diesel exports against 500kt in October and OPEC+ kept December targets unchanged. De-escalation raised 22% -> 23%, re-escalation cut 32% -> 31%.

The energy shock spreads to UK and Swedish policy: the BoE is set to hike 25bp to 4.00% on 5 November with a February follow-up more likely than not (CPI peaking just above 4% early next year on a ~25% energy cap rise, with no second-round effects yet), and the Riksbank is expected to hike 25bp to 2.00% on 4 November despite CPIF ex-energy at 0.5%, then to 2.25% on 3 February, with ING cutting its year-end EUR/SEK target to 11.00. Filed under usd-rates-ai, oil-iran and france-ecb as European tightening; no probability change beyond the entries above.

Still open: US midterms 3 November and Apple's earnings tonight, BoE 5 November, Riksbank 4 November, ING's 2027 rates webinar 4 November, France's promised Fitch review by end-February, Lagarde's successor (de Cos dove vs Knot hawk), Spain's election 29 November, December FOMC on 9 December with payrolls and CPI before it, and BoJ hikes in December and March.

Oil: Brent broke from Friday's $113 settle to well below $100, an 8% drop in a day, as Trump let diplomacy with Iran run and negotiators met Qatari mediators in Doha, with the Democratic sweep adding risk-on relief - so the $100-120 band of the base case no longer holds, though ING notes the war is not over and oil barely moved on the election itself. De-escalation raised 23% -> 29%, elevated premium cut 40% -> 36%, re-escalation cut 31% -> 29%.

France: the National Assembly rejected the revenue side of the 2027 budget unanimously by 458 votes after eleven days, adopted amendments had already added 23.9bn of deficit (5.9% of GDP against the 5% target), the 70-day deadline expires on 18 December with Article 49.3 or a budget by ordinance the only exits, unions mobilise on 5 November, and ING's spread work puts a 150bp OAT/Bund floor with a 200bp Melenchon tail through the April/May 2027 election. Contained-grinding-stress raised 62% -> 63%, French relief cut 10% -> 9%.

US rates: ING's 2027 baseline has the 10y Treasury back above 5.25% (capped at 5.5%) in the first quarter on AI productivity, deficits and sticky inflation before easing to 4.5-4.75% later, while this week's data stayed hot (ADP 86k, ISM services employment at 51.4, payrolls consensus 65k) and the blue-wave tech sell-off was fully recouped. Yields back above 5% raised 32% -> 34%, choppy base cut 38% -> 37%, AI-led risk-off cut 25% -> 24%.

The 2027 outlook suite (good/bad/ugly, euro rates, European spreads, GBP rates, Dutch pensions) is filed without further probability moves: euro rates carry material near-term upside risk with the 10y swap able to break 4% but a 2.5% terminal rate anchoring by end-2027, French spreads are floored near 150bp with the ECB reluctant to deploy TPI, sterling sits above ING's fair value against a 4.75% terminal rate it rejects, and almost 900bn of Dutch pension assets transition in January 2027, keeping the 10s30s curve structurally steeper.

Still open: the 5 November BoE decision (25bp to 4.00% expected, 7-2 vote, February follow-up) and the 5 November French union mobilisation, the 3 November Commodities Feed and FX Daily not yet summarised (kept for tomorrow's --since run), France's 70-day budget deadline on 18 December and the promised Fitch review by end-February, Lagarde's succession (Knot hawkish vs de Cos dove), Spain's 29 November election, the 18 April and 2 May 2027 French presidential rounds, the December FOMC on 9 December with payrolls and CPI before it, and BoJ hikes in December and March.
